summary.text: Factoring out the multiples of \(p\) from the relevant factorials expresses successive binomial ratios as \(\beta_t=\prod_{p\nmid k,\,1\le k<p^r}(1+t p^r/k)\) for \(t=1,2\). A degree-four Newton expansion, combined with doubling and reflection estimates for the inverse power sums, forces the low-valuation terms in \(\beta_2-3\beta_1+2\) to cancel; Wolstenholme-type \(p^3\) bounds for the preceding binomial coefficients then make every remaining cross term divisible to order at least \(3r+3\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\binom{3n}{n}^{2}-27\binom{2n}{n}.
\]
Fix a prime \(p\ge 3\). We prove that, for every \(r\ge2\),
\[
a(p^r)-a(p^{r-1})\in p^{3r+3}\mathbb Z.
\]

We work temporarily in \(\mathbb Q_p\), with the normalized valuation \(v=v_p\), so that \(v(p)=1\). We use the usual conventions \(v(0)=+\infty\),
\[
v(xy)=v(x)+v(y),\qquad v(x+y)\ge \min(v(x),v(y)).
\]
All integers have nonnegative valuation. Since \(p\) is odd, division by a power of \(2\) does not change valuation. We will also use the following elementary observation about the few other denominators that occur: if
\[
d\in\{3,6,15,24\},
\]
then \(p^2\nmid d\). Indeed, if \(p^2\le d<49\), then \(p\) could only be \(3\) or \(5\), and neither \(9\) nor \(25\) divides any relevant \(d\). Consequently, division by any one of these numbers lowers the \(p\)-adic valuation by at most one.

## 1. Reciprocal power sums

For an integer \(m\ge1\), put
\[
N=p^m,
\qquad
S=S_m=\{k:1\le k<N,\ p\nmid k\}.
\]
(The equivalent upper bound \(k\le N\) gives the same set, since \(p\mid N\).) Define
\[
s_j=\sum_{k\in S}k^{-j}
\]
in \(\mathbb Q_p\), and also define the mixed sums
\[
\tau_{ij}=\sum_{k\in S} k^{-i}(N-k)^{-j}.
\]
Every \(k\) and every \(N-k\) occurring here is a \(p\)-adic unit. Thus, initially,
\[
v(s_j)\ge0,\qquad v(\tau_{ij})\ge0.
\]

### The doubling argument

Because \(p\ne2\), multiplication by \(2\) modulo \(N\) permutes the reduced residue system \(S\). If \(a\) is the representative in \(S\) of \(2k\pmod N\), then
\[
a-2k\in N\mathbb Z,
\]
and both \(a\) and \(2k\) are \(p\)-adic units. Hence
\[
a^{-1}-(2k)^{-1}=\frac{2k-a}{2ka}
\]
has valuation at least \(m\). By factoring a difference of powers, the same is true of
\[
a^{-j}-(2k)^{-j}.
\]
Summing over \(S\), and using the fact that \(k\mapsto 2k\pmod N\) is a permutation, gives
\[
v\bigl((2^j-1)s_j\bigr)\ge m.
\]
For \(j=2\) and \(j=4\), this says
\[
v(3s_2)\ge m,
\qquad
v(15s_4)\ge m.
\]
Since division by \(3\) or \(15\) costs at most one power of \(p\), we obtain
\[
\boxed{v(s_2)\ge m-1,
\qquad v(s_4)\ge m-1.}
\tag{1}
\]
We retain the stronger weighted estimate
\[
\boxed{v(3s_2)\ge m.}
\tag{2}
\]

### Reflection identities

The involution \(k\mapsto N-k\) also permutes \(S\). Pairing terms under this involution and simplifying rational functions gives three exact identities:
\[
2s_1+Ns_2=N^2\tau_{21},
\tag{3}
\]
\[
2s_3+3Ns_4+3N^2\tau_{32}
 =3N^2\tau_{41}+N^3\tau_{33},
\tag{4}
\]
and
\[
\tau_{21}+s_3+Ns_4=N^2\tau_{41}.
\tag{5}
\]
For completeness, these are obtained term by term. For example, the sum of \(k^{-1}\) and \((N-k)^{-1}\), followed by adding \(Nk^{-2}\), simplifies to
\[
\frac1k+\frac1{N-k}+\frac N{k^2}
 =\frac{N^2}{k^2(N-k)},
\]
which yields (3). The identities (4) and (5) similarly follow after placing the corresponding terms over the common denominator formed from powers of \(k\) and \(N-k\); summation then gives the displayed formulas.

Solving (4) for \(s_3/3\), we get
\[
\frac{s_3}{3}
=\frac12\left(-Ns_4+N^2(\tau_{41}-\tau_{32})
                  +N^3\frac{\tau_{33}}3\right).
\tag{6}
\]
The three terms in parentheses have respective valuation at least
\[
2m-1,\qquad 2m,\qquad 3m-1.
\]
Here we used (1), the integrality of every \(\tau_{ij}\), and the fact that division by \(3\) loses at most one. Thus
\[
\boxed{v(s_3/3)\ge2m-1,
\qquad v(s_3)\ge2m-1.}
\tag{7}
\]
Now (5), together with (1) and (7), gives
\[
\boxed{v(\tau_{21})\ge2m-1.}
\tag{8}
\]
Finally, solving (3) for \(s_1\),
\[
s_1=\frac{N^2\tau_{21}-Ns_2}{2},
\]
and using (1), (8), and the fact that \(2\) is a unit, gives
\[
\boxed{v(s_1)\ge2m-1.}
\tag{9}
\]
These are the reciprocal-sum estimates needed below.

## 2. A fourth-degree approximation to a finite product

Define the polynomial
\[
\begin{aligned}
F(A,B,C,D)={}&1+A+\frac{A^2-B}{2}
 +\frac{A^3-3AB+2C}{6}\\
&+\frac{A^4-6A^2B+3B^2+8AC-6D}{24}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{10}
\]
This is the expression for the sum of the elementary symmetric functions of degrees \(0,1,2,3,4\) in terms of the first four power sums.

We need a precise error estimate. Suppose a finite family \(f_i\in\mathbb Q_p\) satisfies
\[
v(f_i)\ge c\ge1.
\]
Then
\[
\boxed{
v\left(\prod_i(1+f_i)
-F\left(\sum_i f_i,\sum_i f_i^2,
        \sum_i f_i^3,\sum_i f_i^4\right)\right)
\ge5c-1.}
\tag{11}
\]
Here is a direct proof. Add the factors one at a time. If the old power sums are \(A,B,C,D\) and the new term is \(x\), direct expansion of (10) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(1+x)F(A,B,C,D)
-F(A+x,B+x^2,C+x^3,D+x^4)\\
&\hspace{20mm}
=x\,\frac{A^4-6A^2B+3B^2+8AC-6D}{24}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{12}
\]
If every old term has valuation at least \(c\), then
\[
v(A)\ge c,
\quad v(B)\ge2c,
\quad v(C)\ge3c,
\quad v(D)\ge4c.
\]
Every term in the numerator on the right of (12) therefore has valuation at least \(4c\). Division by \(24\) loses at most one, and multiplication by \(x\) adds at least \(c\). Thus the right side has valuation at least \(5c-1\). The previously accumulated error remains of that valuation after multiplication by \(1+x\), which is integral. Induction proves (11).

For \(t\ge0\), define
\[
\beta_t=\prod_{k\in S}\left(1+\frac{tN}{k}\right).
\tag{13}
\]
Each \(tN/k\) has valuation at least \(m\). Applying (11), and observing that its \(j\)-th power sum is \(t^jN^js_j\), gives
\[
\boxed{
\beta_t
=F(tNs_1,t^2N^2s_2,t^3N^3s_3,t^4N^4s_4)+E_t,
\qquad v(E_t)\ge5m-1.}
\tag{14}
\]

## 3. The binomial recursions

We next connect \(\beta_1,\beta_2\) with the binomial coefficients at consecutive powers of \(p\).

For \(t\ge0\), put
\[
B_t=\prod_{k\in S}(k+tN).
\]
Then \(B_t=B_0\beta_t\) in \(\mathbb Q_p\). To decompose factorials, separate the factors divisible by \(p\): for every integer \(M\ge0\),
\[
M!=p^{\lfloor M/p\rfloor}\lfloor M/p\rfloor!
       \prod_{\substack{1\le k\le M\\p\nmid k}}k.
\tag{15}
\]
For \(M=cN\), the final product splits into the \(c\) blocks
\[
\prod_{\substack{1\le k\le cN\\p\nmid k}}k
=\prod_{t=0}^{c-1}B_t.
\tag{16}
\]
Indeed, in the block \(tN<k\le(t+1)N\), write \(k=tN+u\); divisibility by \(p\) is equivalent to divisibility of \(u\), so its unit factors are exactly those in \(B_t\).

Applying (15) and (16) to the factorial expressions for the binomial coefficients, all powers of \(p\), lower-level factorials, and copies of \(B_0\) cancel. This yields the exact recursions
\[
\boxed{
\binom{2p^m}{p^m}
 =\binom{2p^{m-1}}{p^{m-1}}\beta_1,}
\tag{17}
\]
\[
\boxed{
\binom{3p^m}{p^m}
 =\binom{3p^{m-1}}{p^{m-1}}\beta_2.}
\tag{18}
\]
These identities are in \(\mathbb Q_p\), but both sides are of course rational numbers arising from the indicated integer products.

## 4. First estimates for \(\beta_1\) and \(\beta_2\)

Write
\[
F_1=F(Ns_1,N^2s_2,N^3s_3,N^4s_4),
\]
\[
F_2=F(2Ns_1,4N^2s_2,8N^3s_3,16N^4s_4).
\]
We first establish
\[
\boxed{v\bigl(3(\beta_1-1)\bigr)\ge3m,}
\tag{19}
\]
\[
\boxed{v(\beta_2-1)\ge3m.}
\tag{20}
\]

For (19), substitute (3) into the explicit formula (10). A direct collection of terms gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
3(F_1-1)={}&-N^2(3s_2)+\frac32N^3\tau_{21}
 +\frac32N^2s_1^2+\frac12N^3s_1^3
 -\frac12N^3s_1(3s_2)+N^3s_3\\
&+\frac18N^4s_1^4-\frac14N^4s_1^2(3s_2)
 +\frac18N^4(3s_2)s_2+N^4s_1s_3
 -\frac34N^4s_4.
\end{aligned}
\tag{21}
\]
Using (1), (2), and (7)–(9), every term on the right has valuation at least \(3m\). For example, the first has valuation at least \(2m+m=3m\); all terms with \(s_1\), \(s_3\), or \(\tau_{21}\) have still higher valuation. The denominators here are powers of \(2\), hence units. By (14), \(v(\beta_1-F_1)\ge5m-1\ge3m\), proving (19).

Similarly, using (3), expansion gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
F_2-1={}&N^3\tau_{21}-N^2(3s_2)+2N^2s_1^2
 +\frac43N^3s_1^3-4N^3s_1s_2
 +8N^3\frac{s_3}{3}\\
&+\frac23N^4s_1^4-4N^4s_1^2s_2+2N^4s_2^2
 +16N^4s_1\frac{s_3}{3}-4N^4s_4.
\end{aligned}
\tag{22}
\]
Again every term has valuation at least \(3m\). Division by \(3\), where it occurs, loses at most one valuation, and the stronger estimates for \(s_1\) and \(s_3/3\) more than compensate. The error estimate (14) then proves (20).

In particular, both \(\beta_1\) and \(\beta_2\) are integral in \(\mathbb Q_p\). For \(\beta_2\) this follows immediately from (20). For \(\beta_1\), division of (19) by \(3\) loses at most one, so
\[
v(\beta_1-1)\ge3m-1\ge0.
\]

## 5. Uniform congruences for the lower-level binomial coefficients

Define
\[
A_k=\binom{3p^k}{p^k},
\qquad
C_k=\binom{2p^k}{p^k}.
\]
We claim that for every \(k\ge0\),
\[
\boxed{v(A_k-3)\ge3,}
\tag{23}
\]
\[
\boxed{v\bigl(9(C_k-2)\bigr)\ge3.}
\tag{24}
\]
At \(k=0\), these are equalities with zero, since \(A_0=\binom31=3\) and \(C_0=\binom21=2\).

Suppose first that (23) holds at \(k-1\). By (18),
\[
A_k-3=(A_{k-1}-3)\beta_2+3(\beta_2-1).
\]
The first term has valuation at least \(3\), because \(\beta_2\) is integral. The second has valuation at least \(3k\), by (20), and hence at least \(3\). This proves (23) inductively.

Likewise, from (17),
\[
9(C_k-2)=9(C_{k-1}-2)\beta_1+18(\beta_1-1)
=9(C_{k-1}-2)\beta_1+6\,[3(\beta_1-1)].
\]
The first term has valuation at least \(3\), because \(\beta_1\) is integral, and the second does by (19). This proves (24).

## 6. The decisive cancellation

The separate estimates (19) and (20) only give a congruence of order about \(3m\). The additional three powers needed in the theorem come from the special combination \(F_2-3F_1+2\).

We claim that for \(m\ge2\),
\[
\boxed{v(F_2-3F_1+2)\ge3m+3.}
\tag{25}
\]
To see the cancellation explicitly, substitute (3) and (4) into (10) and collect terms. The exact result is
\[
\begin{aligned}
F_2-3F_1+2={}&-\frac12N^3\tau_{21}
 +\frac12N^2s_1^2+\frac56N^3s_1^3
 -\frac52N^3s_1s_2-\frac52N^4s_4\\
&+\frac52N^5(\tau_{41}-\tau_{32})
 +\frac56N^6\tau_{33}
 +\frac{13}{24}N^4s_1^4
 -\frac{13}{4}N^4s_1^2s_2\\
&+\frac{13}{8}N^4s_2^2
 +13N^4s_1\frac{s_3}{3}
 -\frac{13}{4}N^4s_4.
\end{aligned}
\tag{26}
\]
This identity is just polynomial algebra: expand both copies of \(F\), use (3) to replace the appropriate linear combination of \(s_1,s_2\), and use (4) to replace the appropriate combination involving \(s_3,s_4\).

We now bound every term in (26). From (1), (7)–(9), and the integrality of all \(\tau_{ij}\), their valuations are bounded below respectively by
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{term type}&\text{lower bound}\ \\ \hline
N^3\tau_{21}&5m-1\\
N^2s_1^2&6m-2\\
N^3s_1^3/6&9m-4\\
N^3s_1s_2&6m-2\\
N^4s_4&5m-1\\
N^5(\tau_{41}-\tau_{32})&5m\\
N^6\tau_{33}/6&6m-1\\
N^4s_1^4/24&12m-5\\
N^4s_1^2s_2&9m-3\\
N^4s_2^2&6m-2\\
N^4s_1(s_3/3)&8m-2.
\end{array}
\]
The possible loss of one from division by \(6\) or \(24\) has already been included. For \(m\ge2\), every number in the right column is at least \(3m+3\); the smallest bound is \(5m-1\), and
\[
5m-1\ge3m+3
\]
is exactly where \(m\ge2\) is used. This proves (25).

## 7. Assembly of the desired difference

Set \(m=r\ge2\), and abbreviate
\[
A=A_{r-1}=\binom{3p^{r-1}}{p^{r-1}},
\qquad
C=C_{r-1}=\binom{2p^{r-1}}{p^{r-1}},
\]
\[
x=\beta_2-1,
\qquad y=\beta_1-1.
\]
By (17) and (18),
\[
\binom{3p^r}{p^r}=A(1+x),
\qquad
\binom{2p^r}{p^r}=C(1+y).
\]
Therefore the difference in question is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Delta
&=\left(\binom{3p^r}{p^r}^{\!2}
 -27\binom{2p^r}{p^r}\right)
 -\left(A^2-27C\right)\\
&=A^2x^2+2A^2x-27Cy.
\end{aligned}
\tag{27}
\]
To expose the special cancellation, use
\[
A^2=(A-3)(A+3)+9,
\qquad C=(C-2)+2,
\]
and then replace \(\beta_t\) by \(F_t\) plus its approximation error. This gives the exact decomposition
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Delta={}&A^2x^2
+2(A-3)(A+3)x
+18(F_2-3F_1+2)\\
&+18(\beta_2-F_2)
-54(\beta_1-F_1)
-9(C-2)\,[3(\beta_1-1)].
\end{aligned}
\tag{28}
\]
Indeed, the last four terms involving \(F_t\) and \(\beta_t\) combine to
\[
18(\beta_2-1)-54(\beta_1-1)=18x-54y,
\]
while the second and last terms combine with these to give
\[
2A^2x-27Cy.
\]
Thus (28) is exactly (27), not merely a congruence.

We estimate its six terms.

1. By (20), \(v(x)\ge3r\), and \(A\) is integral. Hence
\[
v(A^2x^2)\ge6r\ge3r+3.
\]

2. By (23), \(v(A-3)\ge3\); also \(A+3\) is integral, and \(v(x)\ge3r\). Therefore
\[
v\bigl(2(A-3)(A+3)x\bigr)\ge3+3r.
\]

3. By (25),
\[
v\bigl(18(F_2-3F_1+2)\bigr)\ge3r+3,
\]
since multiplying by the integer \(18\) cannot lower valuation.

4. By (14),
\[
v\bigl(18(\beta_2-F_2)\bigr)\ge5r-1\ge3r+3.
\]

5. Likewise,
\[
v\bigl(54(\beta_1-F_1)\bigr)\ge5r-1\ge3r+3.
\]

6. By (24), \(v(9(C-2))\ge3\), while by (19),
\[
v\bigl(3(\beta_1-1)\bigr)\ge3r.
\]
Thus the last term has valuation at least \(3r+3\).

Every summand in (28) therefore has valuation at least \(3r+3\), and the ultrametric inequality gives
\[
v_p(\Delta)\ge3r+3.
\tag{29}
\]

Finally, \(\Delta=a(p^r)-a(p^{r-1})\) is an integer. For an integer \(z\), the inequality \(v_p(z)\ge e\) is equivalent to \(p^e\mid z\). Applying this to (29) yields
\[
p^{3r+3}\mid a(p^r)-a(p^{r-1}).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\boxed{a(p^r)\equiv a(p^{r-1})\pmod{p^{3r+3}}}
\]
for every prime \(p\ge3\) and every integer \(r\ge2\), as required.
